catalog_quote: [p. 84] Обязательным, стабильным для всех типов словоформ является повышение ЧОТ в конце словоформы, что позволяет рассматривать финально-слоговой высотный пик как определяющий компонент кумандинского словесного ударения, факультативно сопровождающийся дополнительными компонентами длительности и интенсивности. Итак, анализ экспериментально-фонетического материала позволяет трактовать кумандинское словесное ударение как музыкальное, связанное — локализующееся на последнем слоге словоформы, подвижное — всякий раз при наращении аффиксов перемещающееся (за некоторыми исключениями) на последний слог. [p. 79] Н. А. Баскаков на основании слуховых наблюдений трактует кумандинское словесное ударение как экспираторное, фиксированное, как правило, на последнем слоге слова [10, с. 38]. [p. 81] Таким образом, долготное выделение в определенных позиционно-комбинаторных условиях гласного одного (или нескольких) слогов носит фонематический характер, что опровергает предположение о наличии в языке кумандинцев второстепенного долготного ударения на первом слоге (или на одном из первых слогов).

new_statements.translation: Thus, analysis of the experimental-phonetic material allows Kumandin word stress to be treated as musical, bound — localized on the last syllable of the word-form — and mobile, moving (with some exceptions) onto the last syllable every time affixes are added. [p. 84] ... N. A. Baskakov, on the basis of auditory observations, treats Kumandin word stress as expiratory, fixed as a rule on the last syllable of the word [Baskakov 1972: 38]. [p. 79]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word stress falls on the final syllable of the word-form; when suffixes are added the stress moves to the new final syllable (with some unspecified exceptions). Instrumentally the defining correlate is a pitch peak (rise of F0) on the final syllable, optionally accompanied by duration and intensity; length is phonemic in Kumandin and therefore not the primary stress cue. For the Chalkan variety, Fedina & Širobokova 2019: 47-50 presuppose the general Turkic final-syllable stress and show that contracted verb forms contrast first-syllable stress (present tense, ка́стым 'I dig') with final-syllable stress (past/imperative, касты́м 'I dug').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Seljutina 1998: 80-81 considers and then refutes a hypothesised secondary, obligatorily length-based stress on the initial syllable (the initial long vowels are phonemic/positional length, not stress). Seljutina 2002: 93 and Fedina & Širobokova 2019: 48 mention the general Turkological view of a secondary stress on the first syllable (Fedina cites SIGTJa 1984: 410), not specific to Northern Altai.
new_statements.exceptions: Seljutina 1998: 84 'за некоторыми исключениями' (unspecified); Baskakov 1972: 38 as reported: fixed 'как правило' on the last syllable. Chalkan (Fedina & Širobokova 2019: 48-50, 107, 123): stress on the first syllable of the stem in contracted present-tense forms (ка́стым, ка́штыс, са́тсын, па́ртыр) vs final stress in past/imperative/evidential forms (касты́м, сатсы́н, парты́р); negative past тьурава́ныр stressed on -ва vs positive тьура́ваныр; dual imperative =ак takes stress or not with a meaning difference, =ек always stressed. Radloff 1882 §138 lists general Altai exceptions (predicative/possessive affixes, gerund -ała, participle -attan on the penult, particles).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-form (словоформа) level; instrumental (pneumo-oscillographic) analysis of mono-, bi- and polysyllabic Kumandin word-forms pronounced by native speakers; Seljutina notes the F0 peak on the final syllable is obligatory in all word-form types.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog nort2686 'Northern Altai' (ISO atv) covers three varieties: Kumandin (kumandy-kiži), Chalkan (kuu-kiži, Lebed Tatar) and Tuba (Chern Tatar). The deciding statement (Seljutina 1998) describes Kumandin only; the Chalkan statement (Fedina & Širobokova 2019) is a separate first-hand source on a different Northern Altai variety; nothing was opened for Tuba. Glottolog dialect codes for the three varieties were not verified here (our lists only nort2686).

sources.note: Instrumental study of Kumandin word stress: musical (pitch-peak on the final syllable), bound to the last syllable of the word-form, mobile (moves to the last syllable when affixes are added, with some exceptions); refutes a secondary length-based stress on the initial syllable (p. 81); reports Baskakov 1972: 38 as 'expiratory, fixed as a rule on the last syllable' (p. 79). Image-only scan; pages read from 150-dpi renders.

sources.note: Vowel duration in Altai-kizhi, Tuba and Kumandin bisyllables; invokes Badanova 2011 (Altai: main stress on the last syllable, weaker secondary on the first) to explain Tuba/Altai initial-vowel lengthening; no Northern Altai stress rule of its own.

sources.note: Chalkan: repeats the Turkological view that stress always falls on the final syllable with a secondary stress on the first (citing SIGTJa 1984: 410), then shows that in Chalkan stress has a distinctive function: contracted present-tense verb forms are stressed on the first syllable of the stem (ка́стым 'I dig'), homographic past/imperative forms on the final suffix (касты́м 'I dug'); also pp. 107, 123.

sources.note: Older primary, general to Turkic incl. Altai dialects: every word is enclosed by two tone syllables, a rising half-tone on the first (stem) syllable and the full falling word tone on the final syllable; §138 lists exceptions with Altai examples (predicative and possessive affixes, gerund -ała and participle -attan on the penult, negative verb, unstressed particles).
